title: Twelve Plants
subtitle: How Familiar Crops, Trees, and Alkaloids Remade the Human World

chapters.title: Wheat and the Shortened Stalk
chapters.subtitle: Non-Shattering Ears and Why Dwarf Straw Prevented Global Famine
chapters.historical_anchor: Archaeobotanists Gordon Hillman and Stuart Davies's 1990 Karacadag einkorn domestication trials on the brittle-rachis mutation, paired with Norman Borlaug in Sonora, Mexico (1944–1962) breeding Norin 10 dwarf wheat so nitrogen-fed stalks would not snap under their own grain.
chapters.exit_fact: By halving stalk height with two gibberellin-insensitive genes, Borlaug reduced wind-induced bending torque by half and tripled Mexico's wheat harvest per hectare between 1945 and 1965.

chapters.title: Coffee and the Memory Nectar
chapters.subtitle: How a Mountain Shrub Poisoned Beetles and Bribed Honeybees
chapters.historical_anchor: French naval officer Gabriel de Clieu sharing his daily water ration with a single Coffea arabica sapling in a glass box aboard the ship Dromadaire bound for Martinique in May 1723, paired with Geraldine Wright's 2013 Newcastle University experiments on caffeine and honeybee memory.
chapters.exit_fact: Bees fed nectar laced with natural coffee-blossom concentrations of caffeine were three times more likely to remember the floral scent twenty-four hours later than bees fed pure sugar water.

chapters.title: Corn and the Two-Cell Carbon Pump
chapters.subtitle: How Five Mutations Turned a Stony Wild Grass into a Solar Engine
chapters.historical_anchor: Geneticist George Beadle growing 50,000 teosinte-maize hybrids between 1939 and 1972 to prove that Mexican wild grass (Zea mays parviglumis) became modern corn through five gene mutations, paired with Marshall Hatch and Roger Slack's 1966 discovery of the C4 carbon-concentrating cycle.
chapters.exit_fact: Because corn's outer mesophyll cells pump carbon into sealed bundle-sheath chambers at ten times atmospheric pressure, a field of July maize loses fewer than two hundred molecules of water per fixed carbon atom compared to six hundred in wheat.

chapters.title: The Potato and the Clonal Trap
chapters.subtitle: Andean Freeze-Dried Tubers and Why One Water Mold Broke Ireland
chapters.historical_anchor: High-altitude farmers around Lake Titicaca at 3,800 meters trampling bitter frost-resistant potatoes into freeze-dried chuño across millennia, contrasted with Anton de Bary's 1861 proof that the oomycete Phytophthora infestans destroyed Ireland's 1845 Lumper potato crop because every plant was an identical genetic clone.
chapters.exit_fact: While an Andean farmer plants up to forty genetically distinct potato varieties in a single mountain plot to hedge against blight, nineteenth-century Ireland relied on a single vegetatively propagated clone with zero resistance genes.

chapters.title: Rubber and the Entropic Spring
chapters.subtitle: Smuggled Amazonian Seeds and Why Stretched Polymer Chains Snap Back
chapters.historical_anchor: Henry Wickham chartering the steamship Amazonas on the Tapajós River in June 1876 to rush 70,000 oily Hevea brasiliensis seeds in open rattan baskets to Kew Gardens before they went rancid, paired with Charles Goodyear's 1839 sulfur vulcanization stove discovery.
chapters.exit_fact: Of the seventy thousand Tapajós seeds delivered to Kew Gardens in June 1876, only 2,700 germinated—and just twenty-two surviving seedlings shipped to Ceylon and Singapore parented the plantations that supplied ninety-five percent of the world's rubber.

chapters.title: Cinchona and the Crystal Poison
chapters.subtitle: Andean Fever Bark and How Quinine Drowns Malaria in Its Own Waste
chapters.historical_anchor: Pierre Joseph Pelletier and Joseph Bienaimé Caventou isolating pure quinine from Andean cinchona bark in Paris in 1820, and Aymara bark-collector Manuel Incra Mamani gathering high-yield Cinchona ledgeriana seeds in Bolivia in 1865 for Charles Ledger.
chapters.exit_fact: By grafting Mamani's Bolivian saplings onto hardy red-bark rootstocks in the volcanic soils of Java, Dutch planters raised bark quinine concentrations from two percent to thirteen percent and captured ninety-seven percent of global production by 1930.

chapters.title: Chili Peppers and the Selective Fire
chapters.subtitle: Why Capsaicin Burns Mammalian Molars While Leaving Birds Immune
chapters.historical_anchor: David Julius's 1997 UCSF identification of the TRPV1 heat-pain ion channel and ecologist Joshua Tewksbury's 2001 Tumacácori desert experiments in southern Arizona comparing packrat seed destruction against curve-billed thrasher dispersal of wild chiltepin peppers.
chapters.exit_fact: Zero percent of chili seeds chewed by cactus mice and packrats survived to germinate in Tewksbury's trials, whereas seeds swallowed whole by thrashers and defecated beneath shade trees germinated at higher rates than untouched controls.

chapters.title: Tea and the Bruised Leaf
chapters.subtitle: Robert Fortune's Glass Cases and the Enzyme Switch Between Green and Black
chapters.historical_anchor: Scottish botanist Robert Fortune shaving his forehead and disguising himself as a Mandarin official in Anhui and Fujian between 1848 and 1851 to uncover the processing of Camellia sinensis, and shipping 20,000 living tea seedlings to India inside Nathaniel Bagshaw Ward's sealed glass terrariums.
chapters.exit_fact: Before Fortune used sealed Wardian cases that recycled their own transpired water vapor on deck, fewer than one in a thousand live plants survived the four-month salt-spray voyage from China to Calcutta.

chapters.title: Cotton and the Twisted Ribbon
chapters.subtitle: An Ocean-Crossing Hybrid Seed and the Wire Teeth of Mulberry Grove
chapters.historical_anchor: Jonathan Wendel's genomic discovery that an Old World cotton seed floated across the Atlantic 1.5 million years ago and hybridized with an American wild species to create long-staple Gossypium hirsutum, paired with Eli Whitney's April 1793 wire-tooth cotton gin in Georgia.
chapters.exit_fact: Within ten years of Whitney's 1793 wire-tooth cylinder prototype at Mulberry Grove, annual American exports of upland short-staple cotton jumped from five hundred thousand pounds to forty-one million pounds.

chapters.title: Rice and the Underwater Snorkel
chapters.subtitle: Hollow Root Tubes and the Hibernation Gene That Survives Monsoon Floods
chapters.historical_anchor: How flooded paddy rice builds hollow aerenchyma air channels to pipe oxygen down to submerged roots while suffocating dryland weeds, paired with Pamela Ronald and David Mackill's 1995–2006 isolation of the Sub1A submergence-tolerance gene from an ancient Odisha landrace (FR13A).
chapters.exit_fact: After breeders crossed the Sub1A gene into popular Asian rice varieties without altering grain taste or yield, six million smallholder farmers across India and Bangladesh harvested up to two extra tons per hectare following monsoon floods.

chapters.title: Sugar Cane and the Vacuum Pan
chapters.subtitle: Turgor Pressure Limits and How Recycled Steam Transformed Boiling Houses
chapters.historical_anchor: Open-kettle Jamaica-train boiling houses in seventeenth-century Barbados where cane juice caramelized over roaring wood fires, transformed in 1843 when New Orleans engineer Norbert Rillieux patented the multiple-effect vacuum evaporator.
chapters.exit_fact: Rillieux's triple-effect vacuum chambers lowered the boiling point of cane syrup from above 105 degrees Celsius to 60 degrees Celsius, cutting fuel consumption by seventy percent while yielding white crystalline sugar instead of scorched molasses.

chapters.title: The Oak and the Crooked Knee
chapters.subtitle: Tannin Armor, Plugged Vessels, and the Two Thousand Trees Inside a Warship
chapters.historical_anchor: John Evelyn's 1662 Sylva presented to the Royal Society and Admiral Lord Collingwood planting acorns across Monmouthshire during the Napoleonic Wars to supply curved compass timber for 74-gun Royal Navy ships of the line.
chapters.exit_fact: When ironclad hulls and steam engines replaced wooden warships in the 1860s, tens of thousands of oaks planted after Trafalgar were still only halfway to the century-old maturity required for a warship's hull.
